references.text: The blood from the sacrifice was to be smeared on the horns of the altar, which shows the ritual significance of the horns in atonement rituals.
The incense altar was also to have horns on its four corners, following the same construction principle as the burnt offering altar.
Describes the actual execution of the altar's horns and copper covering, as commanded in Exodus 27:2.
The priest was to smear blood on the horns of the incense altar as part of the sin offering rituals.
Blood was smeared on the altar's horns for a sin offering for the entire congregation.
For a sin offering for a leader, the blood was to be smeared on the horns of the burnt offering altar.
For a sin offering for an ordinary person, the blood was also to be smeared on the horns of the burnt offering altar.
Moses smeared blood on the altar's horns during the consecration of the tabernacle.
Aaron smeared blood on the altar's horns during his first sacrificial service.
Adonijah seized hold of the altar's horns to seek refuge, which shows the significance of the horns as a place of asylum.
Joab fled to the tent of the Lord and seized hold of the altar's horns for protection.
The prophecy that the horns of the altar at Bethel will be cut off shows the altar's horns as a symbol of the power of the worship site.
Ezekiel illuminates the ritual function of the horns, which were constructed according to the instructions in Exodus.
